name: rlarch
description: Eight skills for working in large codebases. dotnet-reflect — inspect any NuGet package or assembly's API surface straight from the DLL on disk: exact signatures merged with XML docs, decompiled method bodies, reverse find-usages read from IL, and version diffs. dotnet-source — ReSharper-style navigation of the .NET solution you're editing, read from .cs with Roslyn, so it sees private members and still works on code that doesn't compile. ts-source — the same shape for the TypeScript/JavaScript project you're editing, read with the TypeScript compiler API: search, outline, JSX-aware find-usages, the module import graph, and dead-code detection that separates what you can delete from what is merely over-exported. orchestrate — execute a plan too large for one context window by delegating every task to subagents, verifying each result against the goal, and re-planning when reality diverges. controller — run a QUEUE of large, mostly independent undertakings (a backlog of bugs, issues, TODOs, migrations): sequence them, brief a nested Claude for each, steer it, verify what it produced independently of its report, land it and record the decisions. One level above orchestrate, which executes a single plan. orchestrate and controller keep their plan, binding rules, evidence and record in WorkState and require it — there is no markdown fallback; without it they stop and point at workstate-setup. nested-claude — run Claude Code inside Claude Code: spawn nested `claude` sessions as background agents with their own context windows, address them by name, drive them over a READY/BLOCKED/DONE protocol, and attach a terminal to watch or unblock one. code-comments — strip comments down to the few that earn their place: a subtractive pass whose default verdict is DELETE, keeping only a present-tense constraint the code cannot state itself, with mechanics for C#/.NET and TypeScript/JavaScript. workstate-setup — get WorkState, the self-hosted MCP server that orchestrate and controller require and the other skills never touch, which holds what coding agents are doing (projects, runs, phases, tasks, claims, evidence, an append-only journal, plus an operator dashboard), running and registered so the work_* tools are callable: it detects which of four states the machine is in and does only the missing part — find or ask for the repo, write the local-only mcp/.env, start the Docker stack, run the one claude mcp add, and prove from tools/list that the tools are really there.
